evidence.title: Emerging algorithmic bias: fairness drift as the next dimension of model maintenance and sustainability
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Fairness gaps by race and sex over time with and without population-level model updating
evidence.effect: Updating restored fairness gaps in some cases (readmission sex gaps) and exacerbated or did not close them in others (pneumonia race gap not closed; ICI gap larger for males); overall performance affected more than fairness.
evidence.quote: During periods of fairness drift, updating models restored fairness in some cases and exacerbated fairness gaps in others.

commentary.bottom_line: One retrospective offline study of 1,739,666 surgical cases tracked fairness gaps by race and sex over time and found that model updating closed some gaps and widened or left others, which suggests that disparities can shift after deployment and that updating alone may not correct them. No study has tested whether scheduled subgroup reassessment against predefined disparity thresholds improves outcomes or reduces disparities.

perspectives.view: The single study (pmid:40079820) is a level 4 retrospective replay in an offline setting with mixed results. It examines fairness gaps under population-level model updating rather than the reassessment practice itself, so directness is limited. With one study, no replication, and no patient outcomes, certainty that the practice achieves its aim is very low.

In the replay, updating restored sex gaps for readmission, did not close a race gap for pneumonia, and enlarged an ICI gap for males. This pattern suggests that a model fix can create new subgroup harms, so a subgroup check after each change may catch errors that aggregate metrics miss. The study did not measure harm reaching patients.

The study reported fairness gaps by race and sex, and aggregate performance changed more than fairness did. Endorsers also name socioeconomic status, health literacy, insurance coverage, and postal code as monitoring dimensions, but no tested evidence covers those groupings.

The study ran on retrospective data outside live workflows, so it offers no information on staff time, data availability for subgroup labels, or how often reassessment can be sustained. CHAI guidance asks systems to define and justify what counts as a significant subgroup shift, yet no study reports how sites set or apply such thresholds.

Eighteen sources endorse the practice, including CHAI assurance guidance at the must level and a lifecycle commentary on generative AI devices that calls for subgroup performance review by postal code. These endorsements rest on expert consensus rather than tested results.

commentary.research_gap: Prospective studies in live deployments should test whether reassessment at set intervals against predefined disparity thresholds detects emerging gaps earlier and leads to corrections that narrow them. Such studies should also report the effort and cost required and should stratify by insurance type, language, and health literacy.
commentary.underserved_note: The only test focused on racial and ethnic minority groups and sex; it did not report results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems therefore have no tested evidence on whether subgroup reassessment detects or reduces disparities for these groups.
